newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese trickle to polls in "landmark" election.
newsitem.headline: Japanese trickle to polls in "landmark" election.

text.p: Japanese voters were slow to go to the polls on Sunday in general elections which Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto hoped would end coalition rule and return his Liberal Democratic Party to sole power.

Political leaders have described the first general election since 1993 as a "landmark" and "turning point" because it will elect a government to lead Japan for the next four years into the 21st century.
"It is widely believed that Hashimoto, 59, will remain at the helm of government after the poll," Japan's Kyodo news service reported on Sunday.
A Hashimoto victory would mark a comeback to its postwar dominance by the conservative and pro-business LDP since it lost power in 1993 because of financial scandals.
The defeat ended 38 years of unbroken LDP rule and set off the last three years of coalition government.
However, what appeared to be a low voter turnout, even in the mainly good weather, cast a cloud over the LDP hopes.
Election officials said in the first four hours of voting the turnout was three percent less than at the same time in 1993's record low turnout.
"I'm worried about the voting turnout. We did the best we could," Hashimoto told reporters on his first public appearance on election day.
Most early voters were elderly, including housewives in traditional dress, and there were few lines at voting booths.

Hashimoto and main opposition leader Ichiro Ozawa, head of Shinshinto (the New Frontier Party), voted earlier in the week, casting absentee ballots in their constituencies because they will be at Tokyo party headquarters on election day.

Polls opened at 7 a.m. (2200 GMT, Saturday) and voting ends at 6 p.m. (0900 GMT). First official results are expected about an hour later with counting ending and a likely result declared about 2 a.m. on Monday (1700 GMT, Sunday).

The election is being held nearly one year ahead of schedule because of Hashimoto's belief that at this time he can win sole power for the LDP because of an improving economy and success in ending a dispute about the presence of U.S. troops on Okinawa.
A record 1,503 candidates from nine parties are contesting the poll, the first held under a new system meant to foster party politics and issues instead of individual pork barrelling.
Under the new system, the Lower House is reduced to 500 seats from 511 and multi-seat constituencies are abolished.
Voters elect 300 single-seat candidates, while 200 seats are decided by proportional representation.
Election officials reported the campaign had been one of the cleanest on record.
They said police had been requested to investigate only 300 incidents of campaign violations compared with 420 in 1993.
Polls forecast a majority by the LDP which led a coalition of the Socialists and the Sakigake party, an LDP splinter group, in the last parliament.
With only 211 seats in the previous parliament, the LDP had to share power with the two smaller parties.
In the main policy difference, Shinshinto, which had 160 seats, opposes an LDP plan to raise the sales tax from three to five percent from April and instead proposes income tax cuts.

Analysts warn the outcome is unpredictable until the last minute, because the possible low turnout due to voter apathy about politics and few differences between the major parties could skew poll forecasts.
The LDP clawed its way into a coalition government one year after the 1993 setback and Hashimoto became prime minister last January.
The balance of power could be decided by the fledgling Democratic Party, formed only last month with 52 Lower House defectors from the Socialists and Sakigake.
